audience: US adults 30-65, financially anxious or curious, skeptical of finance-influencer hype and get-rich-quick framing, wants plain-English explanations of money mechanics they can verify themselves; premium-RPM ad category but also the audience most likely to catch a wrong number

title.formula: [specific, defensible dollar or percent outcome] + [the one plain mechanism behind it] + [who it actually applies to]

mechanism: Why Compounding Works Backwards Against Debt
The Math Your 401k Never Shows You
audience_stakes: For Anyone With a Credit Card

rules: Lead with a real, sourced number - never a rounded-up or invented one. This audience checks.
Resolve the claim in the title. Unlike entertainment's open-loop rule, this audience wants clarity, not a puzzle - an unresolved hook reads as bait here.
Never use 'secret', 'they don't want you to know', 'get rich' - reads as scam-adjacent and is exactly what draws policy/demonetization scrutiny.
Borrowed authority (a named study, a real institution, a real regulation) beats guru authority - the channel has no face and should not invent one.

structure.note: State the number and what it means for the viewer, plainly, in the first 10-15 seconds. No channel intro.
What not knowing this actually costs, in dollars, over a realistic timeframe. Concrete, not vague ('costs you money').
The actual explanation. This is the bulk. One concept per beat, plain language, worked example with real numbers.
Where this does NOT apply, or what it depends on (income level, region, risk tolerance). Non-negotiable trust beat - this is what separates the channel from finance-influencer hype.
What the viewer can actually go check or do this week - numbered, concrete, never a specific buy/sell/invest instruction.
Recap the number, one soft CTA. No 'link to my course/community' hard sell - that pattern is exactly what erodes trust in this niche.

voice_rules: Plain words: 'what you pay' not 'cost basis', unless the jargon term is itself being taught - then define it in the same sentence.
Cite as you speak: 'per the Fed's own data', 'according to your plan's disclosure' - a bare number with no source is a liability here.
Never phrase anything as personalized advice ('you should buy X') - always general mechanics and worked examples ('here is how X works, here is what it would mean if...').
Say 'you' constantly, but keep every claim general - this is the line between education and advice.
script.honesty_guard: This is the highest-compliance-risk niche in the channel portfolio: overclaiming here risks demonetization AND makes the content read as investment advice, which it must never be. Every number must be sourced and defensible; if a claim can't be supported, soften it, never fabricate a source. Never state a specific investment, trade, or product as a recommendation - explain mechanics and let the viewer apply it to their own situation. Never guarantee a return or outcome. Where a topic is genuinely contested (tax strategy, market timing, specific products), say so on screen rather than picking a side. A light on-screen note ('this is general information, not personal advice') belongs on any video that could be mistaken for a recommendation.

images.style: muted editorial photography, paper and ledger textures, real currency macro shots, everyday financial moments - a kitchen-table bill pile, a paycheck stub, a calculator, a bank statement
images._facts_go_on_cards: Every dollar figure, percentage, and rate belongs on a code-rendered stat card, never spoken over an unrelated stock photo - same discipline as robotics-news. This is also an accessibility/trust matter: viewers half-listening should still catch the number by reading it.
